directAnswer: Pope Alexander IV was Rinaldo dei Conti di Segni, a nephew of Pope Gregory IX, who led the Church from 12 December 1254 until his death at Viterbo on 25 May 1261. He is remembered for canonizing St. Clare of Assisi, defending the mendicant friars at the University of Paris, uniting several hermit groups into the Augustinian friars, and continuing the papal struggle against the Hohenstaufen in southern Italy.

sections.h2: A Conti Cardinal and Friend of the Franciscans
paras: Rinaldo was born at Anagni, south of Rome, into the Conti di Segni family that had already given the Church Innocent III and Gregory IX. His uncle Gregory IX made him a cardinal, and he later became cardinal bishop of Ostia. For years he served as cardinal protector of the Franciscan Order, which gave him close knowledge of the friars and of the community of Poor Clares at San Damiano.

When Innocent IV died at Naples in December 1254, the cardinals gathered there chose Rinaldo within days. He took the name Alexander and inherited both his predecessor's unfinished war with the heirs of Emperor Frederick II and an unsettled Rome, where the city's senators and factions often made residence difficult. Much of his pontificate was spent at Anagni and Viterbo.

sections.h2: The Canonization of St. Clare
paras: Clare of Assisi had died in August 1253, and Innocent IV opened the inquiry into her holiness. Alexander completed it, canonizing her at Anagni in 1255, only two years after her death. The bull of canonization praised her poverty and her life of enclosed prayer, and it set the Poor Clares firmly within the Church's official devotion.

His long connection with the Franciscans also shaped his decisions on their behalf. He confirmed privileges for the friars and supported their pastoral work in parishes and universities, even when local clergy objected.

sections.h2: Defending the Friars at Paris and Forming the Augustinians
paras: In the 1250s secular masters at the University of Paris, led by William of Saint-Amour, attacked the Dominicans and Franciscans who held teaching chairs there. William's treatise on the perils of the last times argued that the friars' way of life was dangerous. In 1256 Alexander condemned that work and ordered the university to readmit the mendicant masters, a decision that protected the place of teachers such as Thomas Aquinas and Bonaventure.

The same year he brought together several groups of Italian hermits into a single order under the Rule of St. Augustine, an event known as the Grand Union of 1256. The Order of Hermits of St. Augustine, later simply the Augustinian friars, traces its organized existence to that act. He also extended the authority of Dominican and Franciscan inquisitors in France, continuing measures his predecessors had begun against heresy there.

sections.h2: Manfred and the Kingdom of Sicily
paras: Politically, Alexander's reign was dominated by the question of who would rule the Kingdom of Sicily, which the popes regarded as a papal fief. He continued Innocent IV's plan to grant the crown to Edmund, son of King Henry III of England, but the English were unable to pay or send an army. Meanwhile Manfred, a son of Frederick II, consolidated control and had himself crowned king at Palermo in 1258.

Alexander excommunicated Manfred, but the papacy lacked the resources to remove him. The problem passed to his successors, who would turn to Charles of Anjou. Alexander died at Viterbo in May 1261 and was buried there.

keyFacts: Born Rinaldo dei Conti di Segni at Anagni; nephew of Pope Gregory IX
Elected at Naples in December 1254; reigned until 25 May 1261
Canonized St. Clare of Assisi in 1255
Condemned William of Saint-Amour's attack on the mendicant friars (1256)
Formed the Augustinian friars through the Grand Union of 1256
Died and was buried at Viterbo

faqs.question: Which saint did Pope Alexander IV canonize?
faqs.answer: He canonized St. Clare of Assisi in 1255 at Anagni, about two years after her death in 1253. The cause had been opened by his predecessor Innocent IV.

faqs.question: How did Alexander IV help the Dominicans and Franciscans?
faqs.answer: When secular masters at the University of Paris tried to push the friars out of teaching, he condemned William of Saint-Amour's treatise against them in 1256 and ordered the university to restore the mendicant masters to their chairs.

faqs.question: Why is Alexander IV important to the Augustinian friars?
faqs.answer: In 1256 he united several communities of Italian hermits into one order following the Rule of St. Augustine. This Grand Union is regarded as the formal beginning of the Order of Hermits of St. Augustine.

directAnswer: Pope Urban IV was Jacques Pantaléon, the son of a shoemaker from Troyes in France, who reigned from 29 August 1261 to 2 October 1264. He was Latin Patriarch of Jerusalem when elected, and he is best known for establishing the Feast of Corpus Christi for the whole Church in 1264.

sections.h2: From a Troyes Workshop to the Patriarchate of Jerusalem
paras: Jacques Pantaléon came from modest origins in Troyes, in the county of Champagne; medieval sources describe his father as a shoemaker. He studied in Paris and entered church service, rising through posts that included archdeacon at Liège, bishop of Verdun, and papal legate in Germany and the Baltic lands.

In 1255 Alexander IV named him Latin Patriarch of Jerusalem, a see then administered from the crusader city of Acre. He had come to the papal court on business for the Holy Land when Alexander IV died in 1261. The small college of cardinals, unable to agree on one of their own after three months, chose him though he was not a cardinal.

sections.h2: Transiturus and the Feast of Corpus Christi
paras: At Liège, Jacques had known of the movement begun by St. Juliana of Cornillon, an Augustinian nun who promoted a special feast in honor of the Eucharist. The diocese of Liège adopted such a feast in the 1240s. As pope, Urban extended it to the universal Church through the bull Transiturus de hoc mundo in 1264, fixing it on the Thursday after the octave of Pentecost.

Tradition holds that Urban asked Thomas Aquinas, then teaching at Orvieto where the papal court stayed, to compose the liturgical office for the feast, including hymns still sung today such as Pange lingua and its closing verses Tantum ergo. Popular tradition also connects the decree with the Eucharistic miracle reported at Bolsena in 1263, though the bull itself does not mention it. Because Urban died soon after, the feast spread slowly until it was confirmed in the early fourteenth century.

sections.h2: Charles of Anjou and the Fight over Sicily
paras: Urban inherited the conflict with Manfred, the Hohenstaufen ruler of Sicily. Abandoning the earlier English candidacy, he opened negotiations with Charles of Anjou, brother of King Louis IX of France, to take the Sicilian crown as a vassal of the Holy See. These talks laid the foundation for the Angevin conquest that his successor would complete.

He also strengthened the French presence in the curia, creating a number of French cardinals. In the East, the Byzantine emperor Michael VIII had retaken Constantinople shortly before Urban's election, ending the Latin Empire; Urban both encouraged efforts to restore it and opened contacts with Michael about church union.

sections.h2: A Pope Who Never Lived in Rome
paras: Rome's factional politics kept Urban away from the city for his entire reign. He resided chiefly at Viterbo and Orvieto, and he died at Perugia on 2 October 1264. He was buried in Perugia's cathedral. His three-year pontificate is short, but each year on Corpus Christi the Church still keeps the feast he made universal.

keyFacts: Born Jacques Pantaléon at Troyes, son of a shoemaker
Latin Patriarch of Jerusalem when elected; not a cardinal
Instituted the Feast of Corpus Christi for the universal Church with Transiturus (1264)
Negotiated with Charles of Anjou to take the Kingdom of Sicily
Never resided in Rome; died at Perugia on 2 October 1264

faqs.question: Did Pope Urban IV create the Feast of Corpus Christi?
faqs.answer: He made it a feast of the whole Church in 1264 with the bull Transiturus. The feast had begun earlier in the diocese of Liège, inspired by St. Juliana of Cornillon, where Urban had once served as archdeacon.

faqs.question: Did St. Thomas Aquinas write the Corpus Christi hymns for Urban IV?
faqs.answer: Tradition attributes the office of Corpus Christi, including Pange lingua and Tantum ergo, to Thomas Aquinas at Urban's request while the papal court was at Orvieto. Most historians accept the attribution, though it has been debated.

faqs.question: Why was Urban IV elected even though he was not a cardinal?
faqs.answer: Only a handful of cardinals were alive in 1261, and after three months they could not agree on one of themselves. They turned to Jacques Pantaléon, the Patriarch of Jerusalem, who happened to be at the papal court.

directAnswer: Pope Clement IV was Guy Foulques of Saint-Gilles in southern France, a lawyer and former married layman who became a priest after his wife's death and reigned from 5 February 1265 to 29 November 1268. His pontificate saw Charles of Anjou conquer the Kingdom of Sicily with papal backing, and he is also remembered for requesting the scientific writings of Roger Bacon.

sections.h2: Lawyer, Husband and Royal Counselor
paras: Guy Foulques was born at Saint-Gilles, near the mouth of the Rhône. He trained in law and became a respected jurist and adviser in the service of King Louis IX of France. He married and had children, among them daughters. After his wife died, he entered the clergy.

His rise in the Church was rapid. He became bishop of Le Puy, then archbishop of Narbonne, and Urban IV created him cardinal bishop of Sabina. When Urban died in 1264, Guy was away on a legation connected with the civil strife in England between Henry III and his barons. The cardinals, meeting at Perugia, elected him in his absence, and he accepted after returning to Italy.

sections.h2: The Angevin Conquest of Sicily
paras: Clement completed the policy Urban IV had begun. Charles of Anjou, brother of Louis IX, received the Kingdom of Sicily as a papal fief and was crowned in Rome in January 1266 by cardinals acting for the pope. A month later Charles defeated and killed Manfred at the Battle of Benevento.

In 1268 the young Conradin, the last legitimate Hohenstaufen heir, invaded Italy to recover his inheritance. Clement excommunicated him. Charles defeated Conradin at Tagliacozzo and had him executed at Naples in October 1268, a few weeks before Clement's own death. The episode tied the papacy closely to the house of Anjou for decades.

sections.h2: Roger Bacon and the Opus Maius
paras: Before his election, Guy had learned of the English Franciscan Roger Bacon and his ambitious ideas for reforming learning through languages, mathematics, optics and experimental science. As pope he wrote to Bacon asking him to send his work, despite the restrictions Bacon's order placed on publishing. Bacon responded by composing the Opus maius, along with shorter companion works, and sent them to Clement around 1267.
There is no record of how Clement received them, and he died soon after. Still, the exchange is one of the best known links between a medieval pope and the history of science.

sections.h2: Papal Provisions and a Restrained Household
paras: As a canonist, Clement issued the decretal Licet ecclesiarum in 1265, asserting the pope's right to dispose of all church benefices and reserving to the Holy See those that fell vacant while their holders were at the papal court. Later popes built extensively on this principle.

Contemporaries noted that he avoided enriching his relatives, unusual for his time. He spent his pontificate at Perugia and Viterbo and died at Viterbo on 29 November 1268. The disagreements among the cardinals that followed produced a vacancy of nearly three years, the longest in papal history.

keyFacts: Born Guy Foulques at Saint-Gilles, France; a married lawyer before ordination
Archbishop of Narbonne and cardinal bishop of Sabina
Backed Charles of Anjou, who defeated Manfred (1266) and Conradin (1268)
Requested Roger Bacon's writings, prompting the Opus maius
Issued the decretal Licet ecclesiarum on papal provisions (1265)
Died at Viterbo on 29 November 1268

faqs.question: Was Pope Clement IV married?
faqs.answer: Yes. Before ordination Guy Foulques was a married layman and lawyer with children. He became a cleric after his wife died, which was permitted, and later rose to archbishop, cardinal and pope.

faqs.question: What was Clement IV's connection to Roger Bacon?
faqs.answer: Clement asked the Franciscan scholar to send him his writings. Bacon answered with the Opus maius and related works, which he sent to the pope around 1267.

faqs.question: What happened after Clement IV died?
faqs.answer: The cardinals at Viterbo were divided for almost three years, from late 1268 to 1271. That vacancy ended with the election of Gregory X, who then issued new rules for conclaves.

directAnswer: Blessed Gregory X was Tedaldo Visconti of Piacenza, an archdeacon on crusade in the Holy Land when he was elected on 1 September 1271 after a vacancy of nearly three years; he reigned until 10 January 1276. He convened the Second Council of Lyon in 1274, which proclaimed a short-lived reunion with the Greek Church and adopted his conclave law Ubi periculum.

sections.h2: Elected While on Crusade at Acre
paras: Tedaldo Visconti was born at Piacenza in northern Italy and made his career as a churchman rather than a scholar or bishop. He served as archdeacon of Liège and worked in the circle of influential prelates before joining the crusade led by the future King Edward I of England. He was in Acre in 1271 when news reached him that he had been chosen pope.

The election ended the longest vacancy in the Church's history. After Clement IV's death in 1268, the cardinals at Viterbo were deadlocked between French and Italian factions. Contemporary accounts report that the local authorities shut the electors in and restricted their food to force a decision. Finally a committee of six cardinals agreed on Tedaldo, who was not a cardinal and not yet a priest. He was ordained and consecrated in Rome in March 1272.

sections.h2: The Second Council of Lyon
paras: Gregory's heart remained with the Holy Land, and he called a general council to organize a new crusade, reform the Church and heal the schism with the East. The Second Council of Lyon opened in May 1274. Thomas Aquinas died on his way to it, and Bonaventure, one of its leading figures, died during the sessions.

Envoys of the Byzantine emperor Michael VIII accepted a profession of faith that included the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son, and union with Rome was proclaimed. The agreement had little support among the Greek clergy and people and collapsed within a few years. The council also approved a crusade tithe, though no expedition ever sailed.

sections.h2: Ubi Periculum and the Rules of the Conclave
paras: Having seen the cost of a three-year vacancy, Gregory had the council adopt the constitution Ubi periculum. It required the cardinals to assemble in seclusion ten days after a pope's death, cut off from outside contact, with their food progressively reduced if they failed to elect. The word conclave, meaning a room locked with a key, comes from this arrangement.
Adrian V suspended the law in 1276, but Celestine V restored it and Boniface VIII placed it in canon law in 1298. Its core principles shaped papal elections into modern times.

sections.h2: Ending the German Interregnum
paras: Gregory also worked to restore order in the Empire, which had lacked a generally recognized ruler for years. He supported the election of Rudolf of Habsburg as King of the Romans in 1273, persuaded the rival claimant Alfonso of Castile to give up his claim, and met Rudolf at Lausanne in 1275.

Returning toward Rome, Gregory fell ill and died at Arezzo on 10 January 1276. He was buried in Arezzo's cathedral, where he was venerated locally. Pope Clement XI confirmed his cult in 1713, and the Church honors him as Blessed.

keyFacts: Born Tedaldo Visconti at Piacenza; elected while at Acre in 1271
Election ended a vacancy of almost three years (1268–1271)
Convened the Second Council of Lyon (1274), which proclaimed union with the Greeks
Issued Ubi periculum, the law that created the conclave system
Supported Rudolf of Habsburg as King of the Romans
Died at Arezzo, 10 January 1276; cult confirmed by Clement XI in 1713

faqs.question: Why is Gregory X important for papal elections?
faqs.answer: His constitution Ubi periculum, adopted at the Second Council of Lyon in 1274, required cardinals to be locked in seclusion until they elected a pope. It is the origin of the conclave.

faqs.question: Did the Second Council of Lyon end the East-West schism?
faqs.answer: It proclaimed a reunion after Byzantine envoys accepted a Catholic profession of faith, but the union was rejected by most of the Greek Church and did not last.

faqs.question: Is Gregory X a saint?
faqs.answer: He is a Blessed. His long-standing local veneration at Arezzo was confirmed by Pope Clement XI in 1713.

directAnswer: Blessed Innocent V was Peter of Tarentaise, a Dominican theologian from Savoy who became the first member of his order to be pope. He was elected at Arezzo on 21 January 1276 in the first election held under Gregory X's conclave rules, and he died in Rome five months later, on 22 June 1276.

sections.h2: A Paris Master Beside Albert and Thomas
paras: Peter was born in the region of Savoy and entered the Dominicans as a young man. He became a master of theology at the University of Paris and wrote a widely used commentary on Peter Lombard's Sentences. In 1259 he served with Albert the Great and Thomas Aquinas on the commission that drew up a program of studies for the Dominican Order.

He also governed as provincial of the French Dominicans. Gregory X named him archbishop of Lyon in 1272 and cardinal bishop of Ostia in 1273, and he took a prominent part in the Second Council of Lyon in 1274, where he preached at the funeral of St. Bonaventure.

sections.h2: A Pontificate of Five Months
paras: After Gregory X died at Arezzo, the cardinals gathered there under the terms of Ubi periculum and elected Peter on the first ballot. He took the name Innocent and went to Rome, where he was crowned. In his brief reign he worked to make peace among Italian cities, including between Genoa and Charles of Anjou, and he hoped to carry forward Gregory's plans for a crusade and for union with the Greeks.

Little time remained for larger projects. He died in Rome on 22 June 1276 and was buried in the Lateran basilica. Pope Leo XIII beatified him in 1898, recognizing the long devotion to him, especially among Dominicans.

keyFacts: Born in Savoy; Dominican friar and master of theology at Paris
Helped draft the Dominican program of studies with Albert the Great and Thomas Aquinas (1259)
Archbishop of Lyon and cardinal bishop of Ostia
First Dominican pope; first pope chosen under Ubi periculum
Reigned 21 January – 22 June 1276; beatified by Leo XIII in 1898

faqs.question: Was Innocent V the first Dominican pope?
faqs.answer: Yes. Peter of Tarentaise was the first member of the Order of Preachers elected pope, in January 1276.

faqs.question: What did Innocent V write?
faqs.answer: His main work is a commentary on the Sentences of Peter Lombard, written while he taught theology at Paris. He also wrote biblical commentaries.

directAnswer: Pope Adrian V was Ottobuono Fieschi of Genoa, a nephew of Innocent IV, who was elected on 11 July 1276 and died on 18 August 1276, just over five weeks later. He died before being ordained a priest, consecrated bishop or crowned, and his one notable act was suspending Gregory X's strict conclave law, Ubi periculum.

sections.h2: Ottobuono Fieschi, Legate to England
paras: Ottobuono belonged to the Fieschi, a powerful Genoese family; his uncle was Pope Innocent IV, who made him a cardinal deacon in 1252. His most significant service came in England, where Clement IV sent him as legate from 1265 to 1268 to help restore peace after the conflict between Henry III and the barons led by Simon de Montfort.

At a council in London in 1268 he issued a set of legatine constitutions for the English Church. These decrees on clerical discipline and church administration remained an important part of English canon law throughout the Middle Ages. Among the young men in his household in England was a future pope, Boniface VIII.

sections.h2: Five Weeks as Pope
paras: After Innocent V died in June 1276, the cardinals met in Rome under pressure from Charles of Anjou, who held authority in the city, and elected Ottobuono in July. Still only a cardinal deacon, he went to Viterbo, where he announced that he would revise Ubi periculum, whose harsh conditions many cardinals disliked, and suspended it in the meantime.

He died at Viterbo on 18 August 1276 and was buried in the church of San Francesco there. Because of his short reign, little else can be said with confidence about his plans. Dante places him in Purgatory among those purging the sin of avarice, a literary judgment rather than a historical record.

keyFacts: Born Ottobuono Fieschi in Genoa; nephew of Pope Innocent IV
Papal legate to England (1265–1268); issued legatine constitutions in 1268
Reigned only from 11 July to 18 August 1276
Suspended Gregory X's conclave law Ubi periculum
Died at Viterbo without being ordained priest or crowned

faqs.question: Was Adrian V ever ordained a priest?
faqs.answer: No. He was a cardinal deacon when elected and died about five weeks later at Viterbo before he could be ordained priest, consecrated bishop or crowned.

faqs.question: What did Adrian V do in England?
faqs.answer: As papal legate from 1265 to 1268 he worked for peace after the Barons' War and issued constitutions at a London council in 1268 that long remained part of English church law.

directAnswer: Pope John XXI was Peter Juliani of Lisbon, the only Portuguese pope, who reigned from 8 September 1276 to 20 May 1277. A physician and scholar usually identified with the logician Peter of Spain, he died at Viterbo days after the ceiling of a room in the papal palace collapsed on him. A numbering error means there was never a Pope John XX.

sections.h2: Petrus Hispanus: Physician and Logician
paras: Peter was born in Lisbon and studied, according to most accounts, at Paris. He is generally identified with Petrus Hispanus, author of the Summulae logicales, a logic textbook used in European universities for centuries, and of the Thesaurus pauperum, a collection of medical remedies. Some modern scholars question whether all the works attributed to Peter of Spain are by the same man, so the identification is best described as traditional and widely held.
He served as a physician at the papal court, became archbishop-elect of Braga in Portugal, and was created cardinal bishop of Tusculum by Gregory X in 1273.

sections.h2: Why There Is No Pope John XX
paras: When Peter was elected at Viterbo in September 1276, he chose the name John. Medieval lists of popes had become confused, partly because some counted an antipope and partly through errors that suggested an extra John in the tenth or eleventh century. Believing there had already been twenty popes named John, he took the number twenty-one. The official numbering has never been corrected, so the sequence skips from John XIX to John XXI.

sections.h2: Bishop Tempier and the Condemnation of 1277
paras: In January 1277 John wrote to Bishop Étienne Tempier of Paris, asking him to investigate reports of errors being taught at the university. Tempier went further than an inquiry: on 7 March 1277 he condemned 219 propositions, many drawn from radical readings of Aristotle and his Arab commentators, and some touching positions associated with Thomas Aquinas.

Historians debate how far the pope intended this result, but the Paris condemnation became one of the most discussed events in the history of medieval thought. During John's short reign, the day-to-day direction of papal policy was largely in the hands of Cardinal Giovanni Gaetano Orsini, who would succeed him as Nicholas III.

sections.h2: The Accident at Viterbo
paras: John had a new apartment added to the papal palace at Viterbo, where he could study. In May 1277 part of the structure collapsed while he was inside. He was gravely injured and died several days later, on 20 May 1277. He was buried in the cathedral of Viterbo.
Dante, who admired his learning, places Pietro Ispano among the wise spirits in Paradise, praising his twelve books of logic. He remains the only pope from Portugal.

keyFacts: Born Peter Juliani in Lisbon; the only Portuguese pope
Traditionally identified as Peter of Spain, author of the Summulae logicales
Took the number XXI because of an error in counting earlier Johns
His inquiry led to Bishop Tempier's Paris condemnation of 219 propositions (1277)
Died at Viterbo on 20 May 1277 after a ceiling collapse

faqs.question: Why is there no Pope John XX?
faqs.answer: When Peter Juliani was elected in 1276, confused medieval lists led him to believe there had been twenty popes named John. He took the number XXI, and the numbering was never adjusted, so no pope bears the title John XX.

faqs.question: How did Pope John XXI die?
faqs.answer: Part of a new apartment he had built at the papal palace in Viterbo collapsed on him in May 1277. He died of his injuries several days later.

faqs.question: Was John XXI a scientist?
faqs.answer: He was a trained physician and is traditionally identified with Peter of Spain, who wrote a famous logic textbook and a medical handbook. Some scholars debate whether all those works come from the same author.

directAnswer: Pope Nicholas III was Giovanni Gaetano Orsini, a Roman noble and longtime cardinal, who reigned from 25 November 1277 to 22 August 1280. He issued the bull Exiit qui seminat on Franciscan poverty, secured imperial recognition of papal rule over the Romagna, and made the Vatican a regular papal residence, though he was also criticized for favoring his Orsini relatives.

sections.h2: An Orsini at the Center of the Curia
paras: Giovanni Gaetano Orsini came from one of Rome's great baronial families. Innocent IV made him a cardinal deacon in 1244, and he spent more than three decades in the curia, serving as protector of the Franciscan Order and taking part in many papal elections. Under John XXI he was regarded as the real director of papal policy.
After John's sudden death, the cardinals at Viterbo needed six months to elect him. He was the first Roman-born pope in some time, and he chose to govern from Rome itself.

sections.h2: Exiit Qui Seminat and Franciscan Poverty
paras: The Franciscans were divided over how strictly to live their founder's poverty. In August 1279 Nicholas issued the bull Exiit qui seminat, which explained that the friars renounced ownership of all goods, while the Holy See held title to the property they used. This distinction between ownership and simple use, already found in Bonaventure's writings, was meant to protect both the ideal and the practical needs of the order.
The bull became a cornerstone of Franciscan law. A generation later, its teaching would become the center of a bitter dispute when John XXII rejected the claims some friars built upon it.

sections.h2: The Romagna and the Roman Senate
paras: Nicholas strengthened papal independence on two fronts. In 1278 he obtained from Rudolf of Habsburg formal recognition that the Romagna belonged to the Papal States, greatly enlarging the territory under direct papal rule. He also limited the power of Charles of Anjou in Rome by decreeing that no emperor, king or foreign prince could hold the office of senator of the city.

He began extensive works at the Vatican palace beside St. Peter's and enlarged its gardens, and he restored the papal chapel at the Lateran known as the Sancta Sanctorum. From his time onward, the Vatican increasingly served as the popes' home in Rome.

sections.h2: Nepotism and Dante's Judgment
paras: Nicholas appointed several relatives as cardinals and gave members of the Orsini family important offices in the Papal States. Critics then and later saw this as advancing his family at the Church's expense. Dante placed him in the circle of the simoniacs in the Inferno, a sign of how his reputation was viewed a few decades later.
He died suddenly on 22 August 1280 at his castle of Soriano nel Cimino near Viterbo, and he was buried in St. Peter's.

keyFacts: Born Giovanni Gaetano Orsini in Rome; cardinal from 1244
Cardinal protector of the Franciscans before his election
Issued Exiit qui seminat on Franciscan poverty (1279)
Secured Rudolf of Habsburg's recognition of papal rule over the Romagna (1278)
Barred foreign princes from serving as senator of Rome
Died at Soriano nel Cimino on 22 August 1280

faqs.question: What did Exiit qui seminat teach?
faqs.answer: It held that the Franciscans gave up ownership of everything, while the Holy See owned the goods they used. The friars were allowed simple use without ownership, which preserved their vow of poverty.

faqs.question: Why did Dante place Nicholas III in hell?
faqs.answer: In the Inferno Dante puts him among the simoniacs, reflecting criticism that he used papal power to enrich and promote his Orsini relatives. This is a poet's verdict, not a Church judgment.

faqs.question: What territory did Nicholas III add to the Papal States?
faqs.answer: In 1278 he obtained recognition from Rudolf of Habsburg that the Romagna, in northeastern Italy, belonged to the Holy See.

directAnswer: Pope Martin IV was Simon de Brion, a French cardinal and former chancellor of King Louis IX, who reigned from 22 February 1281 to 28 March 1285. Closely allied with Charles of Anjou, he broke with the Byzantine emperor, and after the Sicilian Vespers revolt of 1282 he excommunicated Peter III of Aragon and proclaimed the Aragonese Crusade.

sections.h2: Simon de Brion, Royal Chancellor and Legate
paras: Simon was born in the region of Brie in France and served King Louis IX as keeper of the seals, or chancellor. Urban IV created him a cardinal in 1261. As papal legate in France he handled the negotiations that brought Charles of Anjou to accept the crown of Sicily, and he later helped prepare the process for the canonization of Louis IX.

His election at Viterbo in February 1281 came after a six-month vacancy and under strong pressure from Charles of Anjou, whose supporters had disrupted the conclave. The people of Rome nonetheless named him senator of the city, an office he delegated to Charles.

sections.h2: Why He Was Called Martin the Fourth
paras: Only one earlier pope, St. Martin I, had actually borne the name Martin. However, medieval scribes had confused the name of the popes Marinus I and Marinus II with Martin, and so Simon took the number four. The official numbering has kept that count ever since.

sections.h2: The Sicilian Vespers and the Aragonese Crusade
paras: Martin's policy followed Charles of Anjou's interests closely. In 1281 he excommunicated the Byzantine emperor Michael VIII, whom Charles intended to attack, effectively ending the reunion proclaimed at the Second Council of Lyon. Charles's eastern plans collapsed, however, when Sicily rose against Angevin rule in the revolt known as the Sicilian Vespers, which began at Palermo on Easter Monday, 30 March 1282.

The Sicilians offered the crown to Peter III of Aragon, whose wife was Manfred's daughter. Martin excommunicated Peter, declared his kingdom forfeit, and offered Aragon to Charles of Valois, a son of King Philip III of France. He granted crusade status to the war that followed. The French invasion of Aragon in 1285 ended in failure, and Sicily remained under Aragonese rule.

sections.h2: A Pope Away from Rome
paras: Unrest in Rome kept Martin in Orvieto and Perugia, where he was crowned and where he spent his reign. He granted the mendicant friars broad rights to preach and hear confessions with the bull Ad fructus uberes in 1281, which caused friction with diocesan clergy.

He died at Perugia on 28 March 1285 and was buried in its cathedral. Dante placed him in Purgatory among the gluttons, mentioning his fondness for eels from Lake Bolsena, a poetic detail rather than a documented record.

keyFacts: Born Simon de Brion in Brie, France; chancellor to King Louis IX
Elected at Viterbo in 1281 with the backing of Charles of Anjou
Excommunicated Michael VIII, ending the union of Lyon
Reigned during the Sicilian Vespers (1282) and declared the Aragonese Crusade
Numbered IV because the two popes Marinus were miscounted as Martin
Died at Perugia on 28 March 1285

faqs.question: What were the Sicilian Vespers?
faqs.answer: A revolt against Angevin French rule that began in Palermo on 30 March 1282. The Sicilians turned to Peter III of Aragon, and Martin IV responded by excommunicating Peter and supporting a French war against Aragon.

faqs.question: Why is he Martin IV if there were only two earlier Martins?
faqs.answer: Medieval lists confused the popes Marinus I and Marinus II with Martin, so Simon de Brion counted himself the fourth Martin. The numbering was kept.

faqs.question: Did Martin IV ever live in Rome?
faqs.answer: No. Because of unrest in the city, he resided at Orvieto and Perugia throughout his pontificate.

directAnswer: Pope Honorius IV was Giacomo Savelli, a Roman noble and grandnephew of Honorius III, who reigned from 2 April 1285 to 3 April 1287. Severely disabled by gout, he governed from Rome, worked to settle the conflicts left by the Sicilian Vespers, and issued a constitution to restrain royal abuses in the Kingdom of Sicily.

sections.h2: A Savelli Pope Elected in Days
paras: Giacomo Savelli belonged to a Roman baronial family and was related to Pope Honorius III, whose name he took. He studied at Paris and was created a cardinal deacon by Urban IV in 1261. Elderly and so crippled by gout that he could not stand and had difficulty using his hands, he was nonetheless chosen quickly at Perugia, only days after Martin IV's death.

Unlike his two predecessors, he lived in Rome, building a residence on the Aventine beside the church of Santa Sabina. His family connections gave him a degree of peace with the city that recent popes had lacked.

sections.h2: After the Sicilian Vespers
paras: Within a year of his election, the chief figures of the Sicilian conflict all died: Charles of Anjou, Peter III of Aragon and Philip III of France. Honorius remained loyal to the Angevin claim to Sicily and did not lift the sanctions on Aragon, but he showed more moderation than Martin IV. In 1285 he issued a constitution for the Kingdom of Sicily that limited taxation and protected the rights of the clergy and people against royal abuses.

He favored the mendicant orders and continued earlier efforts toward a crusade, though none took place. He died in Rome on 3 April 1287 and was buried in the family chapel at Santa Maria in Aracoeli. A long vacancy followed while the cardinals waited out a summer of fever in which several of them died.

keyFacts: Born Giacomo Savelli in Rome; grandnephew of Honorius III
Cardinal deacon from 1261; elected at Perugia in April 1285
Suffered from severe gout throughout his reign
Resided in Rome, on the Aventine near Santa Sabina
Issued a constitution limiting royal abuses in the Kingdom of Sicily (1285)
Died in Rome on 3 April 1287; buried at Santa Maria in Aracoeli

faqs.question: Why did Giacomo Savelli take the name Honorius?
faqs.answer: He was a relative of Pope Honorius III, his great-uncle, and chose the name in his honor.

faqs.question: How did Honorius IV handle the war over Sicily?
faqs.answer: He kept supporting the Angevin claim but took a milder line than Martin IV, and he issued a constitution meant to protect the people and clergy of the Kingdom of Sicily from excessive royal taxation.

directAnswer: Pope Nicholas IV was Girolamo Masci of Ascoli, the first Franciscan to become pope, who reigned from 22 February 1288 to 4 April 1292. A former minister general of his order, he sent John of Montecorvino on the mission that brought Catholic preaching to China, approved a rule for the Franciscan Third Order, and saw the fall of Acre, the last crusader stronghold in the Holy Land.

sections.h2: Successor of Bonaventure as Minister General
paras: Girolamo Masci was born near Ascoli in the Marche and joined the Franciscans young. He served as a papal envoy to Constantinople under Gregory X in connection with the planned church union, and in 1274 he succeeded St. Bonaventure as minister general of the Franciscan Order. Nicholas III created him a cardinal, and he later became cardinal bishop of Palestrina.

When Honorius IV died in 1287, the conclave dragged on for nearly eleven months, slowed by an epidemic that killed several cardinals. Girolamo, who had stayed in Rome through the summer, was finally elected in February 1288 and took the name Nicholas in memory of Nicholas III, who had made him a cardinal.

sections.h2: Missions to the Mongols and to China
paras: Nicholas took a strong interest in the peoples of Asia. He exchanged letters with the Mongol ruler of Persia and received the envoy Rabban Sauma, a Christian monk from China who traveled to Europe and received Communion from the pope in Rome in 1288.

In 1289 he sent the Franciscan John of Montecorvino east with letters for the Mongol rulers, including the Great Khan. John reached Khanbaliq, modern Beijing, in the 1290s and founded the first Catholic mission there, later becoming its archbishop. The mission is one of the lasting results of Nicholas's pontificate.

sections.h2: The Third Order, Montpellier and Santa Maria Maggiore
paras: In 1289 Nicholas issued the bull Supra montem, which gave a formal rule to the Brothers and Sisters of Penance, the lay movement that became the Franciscan Third Order. The same year he granted university status to the schools of Montpellier, and he issued the constitution Caelestis altitudo, which assigned half of the revenues of the Roman Church to the College of Cardinals.

He also left his mark on Rome's churches. He rebuilt the apse of the Lateran basilica and especially of Santa Maria Maggiore, where the Franciscan artist Jacopo Torriti created the mosaic of the Coronation of the Virgin that still dominates the apse. Nicholas chose Santa Maria Maggiore as his burial place.

sections.h2: The Fall of Acre
paras: In May 1291 the Mamluk sultan captured Acre, ending two centuries of crusader presence on the mainland of the Holy Land. Nicholas responded by calling for a new crusade, asking provincial councils to consider uniting the military orders, and seeking help from European rulers, but no expedition followed. His reliance on the Colonna family in Roman affairs also drew criticism.
He died in Rome on 4 April 1292. The cardinals then remained divided for more than two years, a vacancy ended only by the unexpected election of the hermit Pietro da Morrone.

keyFacts: Born Girolamo Masci near Ascoli; first Franciscan pope
Minister general of the Franciscans after St. Bonaventure (1274)
Sent John of Montecorvino to the Mongol court in China (1289)
Gave a rule to the Franciscan Third Order with Supra montem (1289)
Pope when Acre fell to the Mamluks in 1291
Died in Rome, 4 April 1292; buried in Santa Maria Maggiore

faqs.question: Was Nicholas IV the first Franciscan pope?
faqs.answer: Yes. Girolamo Masci, a former minister general of the Order of Friars Minor, was the first Franciscan elected pope, in 1288.

faqs.question: How was Nicholas IV connected to Catholic missions in China?
faqs.answer: In 1289 he sent the Franciscan John of Montecorvino to the Mongol rulers. John established the first Catholic mission in Beijing and later became its first archbishop.

faqs.question: What can visitors see of Nicholas IV in Rome today?
faqs.answer: The apse mosaic of the Coronation of the Virgin at Santa Maria Maggiore, made by Jacopo Torriti, was commissioned during his reign, and his tomb is in the same basilica.

directAnswer: St. Celestine V was Pietro da Morrone, an elderly hermit from the Abruzzo mountains who was elected pope on 5 July 1294 after a vacancy of more than two years. Overwhelmed by the office, he issued a decree confirming that a pope may resign and then renounced the papacy on 13 December 1294. He died in custody in 1296 and was canonized by Clement V in 1313.

sections.h2: The Hermit of Mount Morrone
paras: Pietro was born in the Kingdom of Sicily, in the Molise region, to a peasant family. He became a Benedictine monk and then a hermit, living in caves on Mount Morrone and the Maiella range in the Abruzzo. Disciples gathered around him, and he founded a congregation of hermits following the Benedictine Rule, later known as the Celestines after his papal name.

He was famous for severe fasting and prayer. Before the conclave of 1294 he wrote to the cardinals warning of divine judgment if they delayed further in giving the Church a pope. The deadlocked electors, meeting at Perugia after twenty-seven months, responded by choosing him, though he was about eighty and had no experience of governance.

sections.h2: Coronation at L'Aquila and the Perdonanza
paras: Pietro accepted reluctantly and was crowned at the church of Santa Maria di Collemaggio in L'Aquila in August 1294. He granted a plenary indulgence to all who, having confessed, visited that church on the anniversary of his coronation. L'Aquila still keeps this Celestinian Pardon, the Perdonanza, each year at the end of August.

Under the influence of King Charles II of Naples, Celestine moved the curia to Naples and named a number of new cardinals, many of them French or from the kingdom. He also restored Gregory X's conclave law, Ubi periculum. His inexperience led to administrative confusion, including duplicate grants of the same offices.

sections.h2: The Renunciation of 1294
paras: Within months Celestine concluded he could not carry the burden. After consulting canonists, among them Cardinal Benedetto Caetani, he issued a constitution declaring that a pope may freely resign, and on 13 December 1294 he formally laid down the papacy. His act became the main precedent cited when Benedict XVI resigned in 2013, and Benedict prayed at his tomb in L'Aquila in 2009.
Dante's reference in the Inferno to one who made the great refusal is often read as an allusion to Celestine, though the poem does not name him.

sections.h2: Final Years and Canonization
paras: Celestine hoped to return to his hermitage, but his successor, Boniface VIII, feared that rivals might use him to challenge the new pope's legitimacy. After an attempted flight, Pietro was detained in the castle of Fumone, where he died on 19 May 1296. Rumors later circulated that he had been killed, but there is no reliable evidence for this.
Clement V canonized him in 1313. His feast is kept on 19 May, and his relics rest in Santa Maria di Collemaggio in L'Aquila.

keyFacts: Born Pietro Angelerio, known as Pietro da Morrone, in the Molise region
Benedictine hermit and founder of the Celestine congregation
Elected 5 July 1294 after a vacancy of over two years; crowned at L'Aquila
Granted the indulgence still celebrated as L'Aquila's Perdonanza
Resigned on 13 December 1294; died at Fumone on 19 May 1296
Canonized by Clement V in 1313; feast day 19 May

faqs.question: Why did St. Celestine V resign the papacy?
faqs.answer: He felt unequal to governing the Church and longed to return to the life of a hermit. After confirming by decree that a pope may resign, he renounced the office on 13 December 1294.

faqs.question: Was Celestine V murdered?
faqs.answer: He died in custody at the castle of Fumone in 1296. Rumors of foul play spread afterward, but historians have found no reliable evidence that he was killed.

faqs.question: What is the Perdonanza of L'Aquila?
faqs.answer: It is the annual celebration of the plenary indulgence Celestine V granted to those who confess and visit Santa Maria di Collemaggio on the anniversary of his coronation. It takes place in late August.

directAnswer: Pope Boniface VIII was Benedetto Caetani of Anagni, a leading canon lawyer who reigned from 24 December 1294 to 11 October 1303. He proclaimed the first Holy Year in 1300, issued the Liber Sextus of canon law, and clashed with King Philip IV of France, a conflict that produced the bull Unam sanctam and ended with his seizure at Anagni shortly before his death.

sections.h2: Canonist and Successor to Celestine V
paras: Benedetto Caetani was born at Anagni and trained in law, perhaps at Bologna. He spent his career in papal service, accompanying legations to France and England, and became a cardinal under Martin IV. He was the most experienced lawyer in the curia when Celestine V consulted him about resigning.

Ten days after Celestine's renunciation, the cardinals meeting at Naples elected Benedetto. He returned the curia to Rome and, concerned that his predecessor's resignation might be contested, kept Celestine in custody until his death in 1296.

sections.h2: The Liber Sextus and the First Jubilee
paras: In 1298 Boniface promulgated the Liber Sextus, a sixth book added to the five books of Gregory IX's Decretals. It collected decrees issued since 1234, including Ubi periculum on conclaves and Celestine's ruling on papal resignation, and it became part of the Church's body of law for centuries.

In February 1300 he issued the bull Antiquorum habet, granting a plenary indulgence to pilgrims who visited the basilicas of St. Peter and St. Paul in Rome that year. Large crowds came, and this first Holy Year established the jubilee tradition the Church still observes. In 1303 he founded a university in Rome, the origin of today's Sapienza University. He also canonized King Louis IX of France in 1297.

sections.h2: Clericis Laicos, Unam Sanctam and Philip IV
paras: In 1296 Boniface issued Clericis laicos, forbidding lay rulers to tax the clergy without papal permission. Philip IV of France and Edward I of England, both at war and in need of money, resisted, and Boniface eased the rule the next year. A second crisis began in 1301 when Philip arrested a French bishop. Boniface's protests led to a hardening of positions on both sides.

On 18 November 1302 he issued Unam sanctam. It teaches that there is one holy, catholic and apostolic Church outside of which there is no salvation, describes the spiritual and temporal powers as two swords, and concludes that submission to the Roman Pontiff is necessary for salvation. It is the most sweeping medieval statement of papal authority, and its political claims have been much debated by later theologians and historians.

sections.h2: The Colonna and the Outrage of Anagni
paras: Boniface was also in conflict with the Colonna family, two of whose members were cardinals who questioned his election. He deprived them, proclaimed a crusade against them and had their town of Palestrina destroyed in 1298. The Colonna then allied with the French crown.

In September 1303, as Boniface prepared to excommunicate Philip, the king's minister Guillaume de Nogaret and Sciarra Colonna seized the pope in his palace at Anagni. The townspeople freed him after a few days, but he returned to Rome shaken and died there on 11 October 1303. Philip later pressed for a posthumous trial against him, which Clement V allowed to lapse without condemnation.

keyFacts: Born Benedetto Caetani at Anagni; canon lawyer and cardinal
Elected at Naples 24 December 1294, after Celestine V's resignation
Promulgated the Liber Sextus (1298) and proclaimed the first Holy Year (1300)
Issued Clericis laicos (1296) and Unam sanctam (1302)
Seized at Anagni by agents of Philip IV in September 1303
Died in Rome on 11 October 1303

faqs.question: What did Unam sanctam teach?
faqs.answer: Issued in 1302, it affirms that there is one Church outside of which there is no salvation, uses the image of two swords for spiritual and temporal power, and declares that being subject to the Roman Pontiff is necessary for salvation.

faqs.question: Did Boniface VIII start the Catholic jubilee year?
faqs.answer: Yes. His bull Antiquorum habet proclaimed the Holy Year of 1300, granting a plenary indulgence to pilgrims who visited Rome's apostolic basilicas, and began the jubilee tradition.

faqs.question: What happened at Anagni in 1303?
faqs.answer: Agents of King Philip IV, led by Guillaume de Nogaret with Sciarra Colonna, seized Boniface in his palace at Anagni. Local people freed him within days, and he died in Rome about a month later.

directAnswer: Blessed Benedict XI was Niccolò Boccasini of Treviso, a former master general of the Dominicans who reigned from 22 October 1303 to 7 July 1304. One of the few cardinals who stood by Boniface VIII at Anagni, he sought to calm the conflict with France while condemning those responsible for the attack on his predecessor.

sections.h2: Dominican Master General and Loyal Cardinal
paras: Niccolò Boccasini was born at Treviso, near Venice, and entered the Dominican Order, where he taught and preached before serving as provincial of Lombardy. In 1296 the order elected him master general. Boniface VIII made him a cardinal in 1298 and later cardinal bishop of Ostia, and used him as legate in Hungary.

When French agents seized Boniface at Anagni in September 1303, Niccolò was one of the cardinals who remained with the pope. After Boniface's death, the cardinals elected him quickly, and he took the name Benedict, which was Boniface's baptismal name.

sections.h2: Peace with France and Justice for Anagni
paras: Benedict tried to end the bitter quarrel with Philip IV. He lifted most of the censures that had fallen on the French king and his kingdom and restored some of the Colonna to communion. At the same time he refused to overlook the violence done to Boniface: in June 1304 he excommunicated Guillaume de Nogaret and the others directly involved in the attack at Anagni.

Roman unrest drove him to Perugia, where he died on 7 July 1304 after a reign of about eight months. He was buried in the Dominican church of San Domenico there. Pope Clement XII beatified him in 1736.

keyFacts: Born Niccolò Boccasini at Treviso
Master general of the Dominican Order from 1296
Stood by Boniface VIII during the attack at Anagni (1303)
Lifted most censures on Philip IV but excommunicated Nogaret (1304)
Died at Perugia, 7 July 1304; beatified by Clement XII in 1736

faqs.question: How did Benedict XI respond to the attack on Boniface VIII?
faqs.answer: He reconciled with King Philip IV by lifting most church penalties on France, but in June 1304 he excommunicated Guillaume de Nogaret and the others who had personally taken part in the seizure at Anagni.

faqs.question: Where is Blessed Benedict XI buried?
faqs.answer: He died at Perugia in July 1304 and was buried in that city's Dominican church of San Domenico.

directAnswer: Pope Clement V was Bertrand de Got, archbishop of Bordeaux, who reigned from 5 June 1305 to 20 April 1314. He never went to Rome, settled the papal court at Avignon in 1309, and under pressure from King Philip IV of France presided over the Council of Vienne, which suppressed the Knights Templar in 1312.

sections.h2: An Archbishop of Bordeaux Chosen from Outside the College
paras: Bertrand de Got was born at Villandraut in Gascony, a region then held by the English king as duke of Aquitaine. He studied law, served as bishop of Comminges, and in 1299 became archbishop of Bordeaux. He was not a cardinal.

After Benedict XI's death, the cardinals at Perugia were split between those loyal to Boniface VIII's memory and those favorable to France. After eleven months they chose Bertrand as a compromise. He was crowned at Lyon in November 1305 in the presence of Philip IV and remained in France, eventually settling in 1309 at Avignon, a city just outside the French kingdom and near the papal territory of the Comtat Venaissin.

sections.h2: The Trial of the Knights Templar
paras: In October 1307 Philip IV had the Templars in France arrested on charges of heresy and immorality, and many confessed under torture. Clement first protested the king's action, then issued the bull Pastoralis praeeminentiae in November 1307, ordering rulers throughout Christendom to arrest the Templars and hold their property for the Church.

Papal inquiries followed for several years. Clement's handling of the affair has long been judged weak, since he yielded to steady pressure from the French crown. In 1314, shortly before Clement's death, the order's grand master, Jacques de Molay, was burned in Paris on the king's authority after retracting his confession.

sections.h2: The Council of Vienne, 1311–1312
paras: Clement summoned a general council to Vienne in the Rhône valley. On 22 March 1312, with the bull Vox in excelso, he suppressed the Order of the Temple by apostolic authority, explicitly without a judicial verdict of guilt, and a later bull transferred most of its property to the Knights Hospitaller.

The council also condemned errors attributed to the Beguines and Beghards, addressed disputes over Franciscan poverty, and decreed that chairs of Hebrew, Arabic, Greek and Syriac be established at several universities to prepare missionaries. Clement's own decrees, gathered as the Clementines, were promulgated by his successor in 1317.

sections.h2: Philip IV, Boniface VIII and the French Cardinals
paras: Philip demanded a posthumous trial of Boniface VIII. Clement allowed proceedings to open but let them end without condemnation, and in 1311 he absolved the king of responsibility for the events at Anagni. He canonized Celestine V in 1313 and founded or confirmed universities at Orléans and Perugia.

He named many French cardinals, including several of his relatives, which shaped the Avignon papacy for the next seventy years. Ill for much of his reign, he died at Roquemaure on 20 April 1314 and was buried at Uzeste in Gascony.

keyFacts: Born Bertrand de Got at Villandraut; archbishop of Bordeaux
Elected at Perugia in 1305; crowned at Lyon
Settled the papal court at Avignon in 1309; never resided in Rome
Ordered the arrest of the Templars with Pastoralis praeeminentiae (1307)
Convened the Council of Vienne and suppressed the Templars with Vox in excelso (1312)
Canonized Celestine V (1313); died 20 April 1314

faqs.question: Why did Clement V move the papacy to Avignon?
faqs.answer: Central Italy was unsettled, and Clement remained in France after his coronation at Lyon, partly to deal with Philip IV over the Templars and Boniface VIII. In 1309 he settled at Avignon, near papal lands in the Comtat Venaissin.

faqs.question: Did Clement V find the Knights Templar guilty?
faqs.answer: No. At the Council of Vienne in 1312 he suppressed the order by apostolic decision in Vox in excelso, stating that this was not a judicial condemnation. Its property was largely given to the Hospitallers.

faqs.question: What else did the Council of Vienne decide?
faqs.answer: Besides the Templars, it addressed Franciscan poverty, condemned errors attributed to the Beguines and Beghards, and called for teaching Hebrew, Arabic, Greek and Syriac at universities.

directAnswer: Pope John XXII was Jacques Duèze of Cahors, elected at Lyon on 7 August 1316 at about seventy-two, who reigned at Avignon until 4 December 1334. A tireless administrator, he reorganized papal finances, canonized Thomas Aquinas, and condemned the Franciscan teaching that Christ and the apostles owned nothing. He also stirred controversy with sermons on the beatific vision, which he retracted before his death.

sections.h2: Elected After a Two-Year Vacancy
paras: Jacques Duèze was born at Cahors in southern France and studied law. He served the Angevin kings of Naples as chancellor, became bishop of Fréjus and then of Avignon, and was created a cardinal by Clement V. After Clement's death the cardinals were divided for more than two years until they were assembled at Lyon in 1316 and chose him.
Many expected a brief transitional reign from a man in his seventies. Instead he governed for eighteen years and became one of the most energetic popes of the Middle Ages.

sections.h2: Centralizing the Avignon Curia
paras: John reorganized the papal administration and finances, expanding the system of reserved benefices and fees that funded the curia. He created new dioceses in southern France and elsewhere and organized the papal court at Avignon. He also promulgated the Clementines, the canonical collection of his predecessor, in 1317, and his own decrees circulated as the Extravagantes.
In 1323 he canonized Thomas Aquinas. In 1329 he condemned a series of propositions drawn from the writings of the Dominican Meister Eckhart in the bull In agro dominico.

sections.h2: Franciscan Poverty, Ockham and Louis of Bavaria
paras: John confronted the Spiritual Franciscans and then the whole order over poverty. In 1322 he renounced papal ownership of Franciscan goods, undermining the arrangement set by Nicholas III, and in the bull Cum inter nonnullos of 1323 he declared it heretical to assert that Christ and the apostles had owned nothing at all.

The minister general Michael of Cesena and the philosopher William of Ockham fled to the court of Louis of Bavaria, whom John refused to recognize as emperor. Ockham wrote extensively against the pope's authority. Louis was crowned in Rome in 1328 by lay representatives and set up an antipope, Nicholas V, who submitted to John in 1330.

sections.h2: The Beatific Vision Controversy
paras: From 1331 John preached that the souls of the blessed would not see God face to face until after the Last Judgment, enjoying in the meantime only the vision of Christ's humanity. He presented this as his opinion as a theologian rather than as a definition, but it met strong opposition from theologians in Paris and elsewhere.

Shortly before his death, John declared that the purified souls of the faithful departed see the divine essence clearly, so far as their state allows, and submitted his views to the judgment of the Church. He died at Avignon on 4 December 1334. His successor, Benedict XII, settled the question with the constitution Benedictus Deus.

keyFacts: Born Jacques Duèze at Cahors; former bishop of Avignon
Elected at Lyon in 1316 after a vacancy of more than two years
Reigned eighteen years at Avignon and reorganized papal finances
Canonized Thomas Aquinas (1323)
Condemned the doctrine of the absolute poverty of Christ in Cum inter nonnullos (1323)
Retracted his beatific vision opinion before dying on 4 December 1334

faqs.question: Did Pope John XXII teach heresy about heaven?
faqs.answer: He preached, as a private theological opinion, that the saved would not see God fully until the Last Judgment. It was never defined, he retracted it before his death in 1334, and Benedict XII's Benedictus Deus defined the opposite.

faqs.question: Why did William of Ockham oppose John XXII?
faqs.answer: John rejected the Franciscan claim that Christ and the apostles owned nothing. Ockham, siding with the Franciscan minister general Michael of Cesena, fled to Louis of Bavaria and wrote against the pope's authority.

faqs.question: Which saint did John XXII canonize?
faqs.answer: He canonized St. Thomas Aquinas in 1323, less than fifty years after the Dominican theologian's death.

directAnswer: Pope Benedict XII was Jacques Fournier, a Cistercian monk and former bishop of Pamiers, who reigned at Avignon from 20 December 1334 to 25 April 1342. He issued the constitution Benedictus Deus defining that the souls of the just see God immediately after death and purification, reformed the religious orders, and opposed nepotism.

sections.h2: The White Cardinal from the County of Foix
paras: Jacques Fournier was born at Saverdun in the county of Foix and became a Cistercian monk, studying theology in Paris and later serving as abbot of Fontfroide. As bishop of Pamiers from 1317, he personally conducted a detailed inquisition into Cathar beliefs in his diocese. The register of those interrogations survives and is a rich source for the daily life of medieval villagers, especially in the village of Montaillou.

John XXII made him bishop of Mirepoix and then cardinal in 1327. Because he kept wearing his white Cistercian habit, he was known as the White Cardinal. He served as a leading theologian in the curia and helped prepare the response to John XXII's beatific vision sermons.

sections.h2: Benedictus Deus
paras: Elected on 20 December 1334, Benedict moved quickly to resolve the controversy his predecessor had raised. In the constitution Benedictus Deus, issued in January 1336, he defined that the souls of the saints and of the faithful who need no further purification, or who have completed it, see the divine essence face to face immediately after death, without waiting for the resurrection of the body.
The constitution also taught that those who die in mortal sin go down to hell immediately. Benedictus Deus remains a basic text of Catholic teaching on the last things.

sections.h2: Reforming Monks, Friars and the Curia
paras: A monk himself, Benedict issued reform constitutions for several orders: for the Cistercians in 1335, for the Benedictines in 1336 in a document often called the Benedictina, for the Franciscans in 1336, and for the canons regular in 1339. These addressed discipline, finances and the education of members.

He sent clergy who lingered at Avignon seeking favors back to their dioceses, tightened procedures for granting benefices, and refused to advance his relatives, a marked contrast with other popes of the period.

sections.h2: The Palace of the Popes
paras: Benedict considered returning to Rome and spent money repairing St. Peter's and the Lateran, but war in Italy and the tensions that led to the Hundred Years' War kept him in Avignon. He began building the fortress-like Palace of the Popes there, the section now called the Old Palace.
His efforts to make peace between France and England did not succeed, and his attempts at reconciliation with Louis of Bavaria failed. He died at Avignon on 25 April 1342.

keyFacts: Born Jacques Fournier at Saverdun; Cistercian monk
As bishop of Pamiers, kept the inquisition register that documents Montaillou
Issued Benedictus Deus on the beatific vision (1336)
Wrote reform constitutions for Cistercians, Benedictines, Franciscans and canons regular
Began the Palace of the Popes at Avignon
Died at Avignon on 25 April 1342

faqs.question: What did Benedictus Deus define?
faqs.answer: It defined that the souls of the just who have no need of purification, or who have been purified, see God face to face immediately after death, before the final resurrection.

faqs.question: What is the Fournier Register?
faqs.answer: It is the record of the inquisition Jacques Fournier conducted as bishop of Pamiers in the 1310s and 1320s. Its detailed testimonies, especially from Montaillou, are valued by historians of medieval daily life.

faqs.question: Why was Benedict XII called the White Cardinal?
faqs.answer: As a Cistercian he continued to wear the order's white habit after being made a cardinal in 1327.

directAnswer: Pope Clement VI was Pierre Roger, a Benedictine theologian and celebrated preacher who reigned at Avignon from 7 May 1342 to 6 December 1352. He led the Church through the Black Death, defended Jews falsely blamed for the plague, purchased Avignon for the papacy, and set the jubilee interval at fifty years.

sections.h2: Pierre Roger, Preacher and Archbishop
paras: Pierre Roger was born at Maumont in the Limousin and entered the Benedictine abbey of La Chaise-Dieu as a boy. He became a master of theology at Paris and won fame as a preacher. He served as abbot of Fécamp, then archbishop of Sens and of Rouen, and was an adviser to King Philip VI of France. Benedict XII created him a cardinal in 1338.

Elected in May 1342, he took a very different approach from his austere predecessor. He was generous toward petitioners, made his court a center of art and learning, and enlarged the Palace of the Popes with the New Palace and its great chapel.

sections.h2: Pope During the Black Death
paras: The plague reached Avignon early in 1348 and killed a large part of the city's population. Clement stayed in the city, consulted physicians, and granted a plenary indulgence to the dying who repented. When cemeteries filled, he consecrated the Rhône so that bodies could be committed to the river.

As Jews were accused of causing the plague and massacred in many places, Clement issued bulls in 1348 forbidding violence against them. He pointed out that Jews were dying of the plague like everyone else and in regions where no Jews lived, and he ordered clergy to protect them. In 1349 he also condemned the flagellant movement that spread in the plague's wake.

sections.h2: Unigenitus and the Jubilee of 1350
paras: In the bull Unigenitus of 1343, Clement set the interval between Holy Years at fifty years instead of one hundred, so that more of the faithful could gain the jubilee indulgence. The bull also gave a classic explanation of the treasury of merit drawn from Christ and the saints. Pilgrims came to Rome in large numbers for the jubilee of 1350, though the pope remained at Avignon.

sections.h2: Avignon, Rome and the Empire
paras: In 1348 Clement purchased the city of Avignon from Queen Joanna I of Naples, countess of Provence, making it papal property. In Rome, he at first approved and then turned against Cola di Rienzo, who seized power in 1347 proclaiming the revival of the Roman republic.

He opposed Louis of Bavaria and supported the election of Charles IV of Luxembourg as King of the Romans in 1346. He also helped organize a naval league that captured Smyrna in 1344. Clement's lavish spending and his promotion of relatives drew criticism, including from the poet Petrarch. He died at Avignon on 6 December 1352 and was buried at La Chaise-Dieu.

keyFacts: Born Pierre Roger at Maumont; Benedictine monk of La Chaise-Dieu
Archbishop of Rouen and renowned preacher before his election in 1342
Stayed at Avignon through the Black Death (1348) and protected Jews from accusations
Set the jubilee interval at fifty years with Unigenitus (1343)
Purchased Avignon from Queen Joanna I of Naples (1348)
Died at Avignon on 6 December 1352

faqs.question: What did Clement VI do during the Black Death?
faqs.answer: He stayed in Avignon, granted a plenary indulgence to dying penitents, consecrated the Rhône for burials when cemeteries were full, and issued bulls forbidding the persecution of Jews blamed for the plague.

faqs.question: How did Avignon become papal property?
faqs.answer: Clement VI bought the city in 1348 from Queen Joanna I of Naples, who held it as countess of Provence.

faqs.question: Why was the 1350 jubilee held only fifty years after the first?
faqs.answer: In 1343 Clement VI's bull Unigenitus reduced the interval between Holy Years from one hundred to fifty years.

directAnswer: Pope Innocent VI was Étienne Aubert, a French law professor and cardinal who reigned at Avignon from 18 December 1352 to 12 September 1362. He cut back the luxury of the Avignon court, sent Cardinal Gil de Albornoz to restore papal government in Italy, and supported the diplomacy that produced the Treaty of Brétigny between France and England in 1360.

sections.h2: Étienne Aubert of the Limousin
paras: Étienne Aubert was born at Les Monts, near Beyssac in the Limousin. He taught civil law at Toulouse and served in royal administration before becoming bishop of Noyon and then of Clermont. Clement VI made him a cardinal in 1342.

Before electing him, the cardinals signed an agreement limiting the future pope's powers in their favor. Innocent accepted it at first but declared it invalid in 1353, holding that cardinals could not bind a pope in this way.

sections.h2: Austerity at Avignon and Albornoz in Italy
paras: In contrast with Clement VI, Innocent reduced spending, dismissed many members of the court, and ordered clergy holding benefices to reside in them. He continued action against the radical Franciscan groups known as Fraticelli.

His most consequential decision was to send the Spanish cardinal Gil Álvarez de Albornoz to Italy as legate in 1353. Through military campaigns and negotiation, Albornoz restored papal authority across much of the Papal States, and his legal code, the Egidian Constitutions of 1357, governed the territory for centuries. In 1355 a papal legate crowned Charles IV emperor in Rome.

sections.h2: War, Free Companies and Brétigny
paras: The Hundred Years' War weighed on his reign. After the English captured King John II of France at Poitiers in 1356, papal envoys worked for peace, and their efforts contributed to the Treaty of Brétigny in 1360. Bands of unemployed soldiers, the free companies, then threatened Avignon itself, and Innocent had the city's walls strengthened and paid ransoms to keep them away.
He also founded a Carthusian monastery at Villeneuve-lès-Avignon, where he was buried after his death on 12 September 1362.

keyFacts: Born Étienne Aubert at Les Monts in the Limousin; professor of law at Toulouse
Cardinal from 1342; elected at Avignon in December 1352
Annulled the cardinals' electoral agreement limiting papal power (1353)
Sent Cardinal Albornoz to restore the Papal States; Egidian Constitutions (1357)
Papal diplomacy aided the Treaty of Brétigny (1360)
Died 12 September 1362; buried at the Carthusian monastery of Villeneuve-lès-Avignon

faqs.question: Who was Cardinal Albornoz and why did Innocent VI send him to Italy?
faqs.answer: Gil Álvarez de Albornoz was a Spanish cardinal and former archbishop of Toledo. Innocent sent him in 1353 to recover control of the Papal States, which he did over the following years, issuing the Egidian Constitutions in 1357.

faqs.question: What role did Innocent VI play in the Hundred Years' War?
faqs.answer: He sent envoys to mediate between France and England, and their work helped bring about the Treaty of Brétigny in 1360, a temporary peace.

directAnswer: Blessed Urban V was Guillaume de Grimoard, a Benedictine abbot who was elected on 28 September 1362 without being a cardinal and reigned until 19 December 1370. He returned the papacy to Rome in 1367, received the Byzantine emperor's personal profession of faith there, and founded and supported universities, but went back to Avignon shortly before his death. Pius IX beatified him in 1870.

sections.h2: A Benedictine Abbot and Canonist
paras: Guillaume de Grimoard was born at the castle of Grizac in the region of Lozère in southern France. He became a Benedictine monk, studied and taught canon law at Montpellier, Toulouse, Paris and Avignon, and served as abbot of Saint-Germain at Auxerre and then of Saint-Victor in Marseille. He was on a diplomatic mission in Naples when the cardinals, unable to agree on one of their own, chose him in 1362.
As pope he kept the Benedictine habit and the rhythm of monastic life. He reduced the luxury of the court, opposed the accumulation of benefices, and pressed for the reform of clergy and religious.

sections.h2: Patron of Students and Universities
paras: Urban was deeply committed to education. He supported large numbers of poor students at his own expense, endowed colleges at Montpellier, and approved the founding of universities at Kraków in 1364 and Vienna in 1365, among others. He also encouraged missionary work in eastern Europe and Asia.

His reign coincided with crusading expeditions to the eastern Mediterranean, including the sack of Alexandria by King Peter I of Cyprus in 1365 and the campaign of Count Amadeus VI of Savoy in 1366, which Urban encouraged as responses to Turkish and Mamluk power.

sections.h2: The Return to Rome, 1367–1370
paras: Against the wishes of most of his French cardinals, Urban left Avignon and entered Rome in October 1367, the first pope to reside there in some sixty years. He began restoring its neglected churches, and in 1368 he placed the relics venerated as the heads of Sts. Peter and Paul in new reliquaries at the Lateran. Emperor Charles IV visited him in 1368.
In 1369 the Byzantine emperor John V Palaiologos came to Rome and made a personal profession of the Catholic faith before the pope, though it did not bring about a union of the churches.

sections.h2: Going Back to Avignon
paras: Instability in the Papal States and war between France and England led Urban to return to Avignon in September 1370, despite appeals to remain, including from St. Bridget of Sweden. He died there on 19 December 1370, only months after his arrival. His remains were later moved to the abbey of Saint-Victor in Marseille.
Miracles were reported at his tomb, and his reputation for holiness grew. Pope Pius IX beatified him in 1870.

keyFacts: Born Guillaume de Grimoard at Grizac, France; Benedictine abbot of Saint-Victor, Marseille
Elected in 1362 though not a cardinal
Supported poor students and the founding of the universities of Kraków and Vienna
Returned to Rome in 1367; received John V Palaiologos's profession of faith (1369)
Went back to Avignon in 1370 and died there on 19 December 1370
Beatified by Pius IX in 1870

faqs.question: Did Urban V move the papacy back to Rome?
faqs.answer: He resided in Rome from 1367 to 1370, the first pope to do so in decades, but returned to Avignon in 1370. The lasting return came under his successor, Gregory XI, in 1377.

faqs.question: Why is Urban V a Blessed?
faqs.answer: He was known for his holy, monastic way of life and concern for the poor and for students, and miracles were reported at his tomb. Pope Pius IX beatified him in 1870.

faqs.question: Which universities did Urban V help found?
faqs.answer: He approved the founding of the universities of Kraków (1364) and Vienna (1365), and he supported colleges and poor scholars at Montpellier and elsewhere.

directAnswer: Pope Gregory XI was Pierre Roger de Beaufort, a nephew of Clement VI, who reigned from 30 December 1370 to 27 March 1378. Urged on by St. Catherine of Siena among others, he ended the Avignon residence by entering Rome in January 1377. He was the last French pope, and his death in Rome led to the disputed election that began the Western Schism.

sections.h2: A Cardinal at Nineteen
paras: Pierre Roger de Beaufort was born at Maumont in the Limousin, the same place as his uncle Pope Clement VI, who made him a cardinal in 1348 while he was still a young man. He then studied law at Perugia under the jurist Baldus de Ubaldis and gained a reputation for learning and piety.

After Urban V's death, the cardinals at Avignon elected him unanimously at the end of December 1370. He was only a deacon and was ordained priest and consecrated before his coronation in January 1371.

sections.h2: The War of the Eight Saints
paras: Gregory's plans for returning to Italy were complicated by conflict with Florence, which feared papal expansion and stirred revolt in the Papal States in 1375. The Florentine war council, known as the Eight Saints, gave the war its name. Gregory placed Florence under interdict in 1376, which damaged the city's trade across Europe.

Papal mercenaries under Cardinal Robert of Geneva carried out the brutal sack of Cesena in 1377, a massacre that horrified contemporaries and tarnished the papal cause. Robert would later become the first Avignon antipope, Clement VII.

sections.h2: St. Catherine of Siena and the Return to Rome
paras: Many voices called on the pope to return to the see of Peter, including St. Bridget of Sweden before her death in 1373 and above all St. Catherine of Siena. Catherine wrote him a series of letters urging reform, peace with Florence and a return to Rome, and in 1376 she traveled to Avignon to speak with him in person.

Gregory left Avignon in September 1376 and, after a difficult journey by sea and land, entered Rome on 17 January 1377. He took up residence at the Vatican, which from then on became the main papal residence.

sections.h2: Wycliffe, Death in Rome and the Coming Schism
paras: In 1377 Gregory issued bulls condemning nineteen propositions taken from the writings of the English theologian John Wycliffe and ordering an investigation of his teaching in England.

Rome proved unsettled, and Gregory considered returning to Avignon, but he fell ill and died on 27 March 1378. He was buried in the church of Santa Maria Nova, now Santa Francesca Romana. The conclave that followed, held in Rome under heavy popular pressure, elected Urban VI, whose contested election opened the Great Western Schism. No Frenchman has been pope since.

keyFacts: Born Pierre Roger de Beaufort at Maumont; nephew of Clement VI
Made a cardinal by his uncle in 1348; studied law at Perugia
Placed Florence under interdict during the War of the Eight Saints (1376)
Encouraged by St. Catherine of Siena, entered Rome on 17 January 1377
Condemned propositions of John Wycliffe (1377)
Died in Rome, 27 March 1378; the last French pope

faqs.question: What role did St. Catherine of Siena play in Gregory XI's return to Rome?
faqs.answer: She wrote him many letters and visited him at Avignon in 1376, urging him to return to Rome, reform the Church and make peace. He left Avignon that autumn and reached Rome in January 1377.

faqs.question: Was Gregory XI the last French pope?
faqs.answer: Yes. No pope from France has been elected since his death in 1378.

faqs.question: How is Gregory XI connected to the Western Schism?
faqs.answer: He died in Rome in 1378, and the tense conclave that followed elected Urban VI. Months later, dissatisfied cardinals declared that election invalid and chose a rival, beginning the schism.

directAnswer: Pope Urban VI was Bartolomeo Prignano, archbishop of Bari, elected in Rome on 8 April 1378 and reigning until 15 October 1389. He was the last pope elected from outside the College of Cardinals. His harsh treatment of the cardinals led a group of them to declare his election invalid and elect a rival, Clement VII, beginning the Great Western Schism.

sections.h2: Archbishop of Bari and Head of the Chancery
paras: Bartolomeo Prignano was born in Naples and made his career in the papal administration at Avignon, where he became known as an able and austere official. He was named archbishop of Bari in 1377 and directed the papal chancery after Gregory XI returned to Rome.

At the conclave of April 1378, crowds outside the Vatican demanded a Roman or at least an Italian pope. The cardinals chose Prignano, a Neapolitan who was not a cardinal and was expected to be manageable. During the voting the crowd broke in, and the cardinals briefly fled, but in the following weeks they treated him as pope, attended his coronation and asked him for favors.

sections.h2: The Election Contested and the Schism Begins
paras: Urban set out at once to reform the curia, but he did so with a violent temper, publicly rebuking cardinals for their wealth and conduct. Within months most of the French cardinals withdrew to Anagni and in August 1378 declared that his election had been made under fear and was therefore void. In September at Fondi they elected Cardinal Robert of Geneva, who took the name Clement VII and later settled at Avignon.
