Western Christendom divided. France, Scotland, Naples and later the Spanish kingdoms recognized Clement, while England, most of the Empire, Hungary and much of Italy remained with Urban. St. Catherine of Siena strongly supported Urban and came to Rome to aid his cause before her death in 1380. The Church has since regarded the Roman line as the legitimate one.

sections.h2: Naples and the Cardinals of Nocera
paras: Queen Joanna I of Naples backed Clement, so Urban declared her deposed and invested Charles of Durazzo with the kingdom. Charles took Naples, and Joanna was killed in 1382. Urban soon quarreled with Charles as well and was besieged by him at Nocera in 1385.

There Urban accused several cardinals of conspiring against him and had six arrested and tortured. Five of them were never seen again and are generally believed to have been put to death. The episode further damaged his standing even among his own supporters.

sections.h2: The Visitation and the Jubilee
paras: In 1389 Urban decided to extend the Feast of the Visitation of the Blessed Virgin Mary to the whole Church, a decree published by his successor. He also reduced the interval between jubilees to thirty-three years, the traditional length of Christ's life, and proclaimed a Holy Year for 1390.
He died in Rome on 15 October 1389 and was buried in St. Peter's. The cardinals of his obedience elected a successor, and the schism continued for nearly three more decades.

keyFacts: Born Bartolomeo Prignano in Naples; archbishop of Bari
Elected 8 April 1378 amid Roman crowds demanding an Italian pope
Last pope chosen from outside the College of Cardinals
Dissenting cardinals elected Clement VII in September 1378, beginning the Western Schism
Decided to extend the Feast of the Visitation to the universal Church (1389)
Died in Rome on 15 October 1389

faqs.question: Was Urban VI a legitimate pope?
faqs.answer: The Catholic Church counts Urban VI and his Roman successors as the legitimate popes of the Western Schism. The cardinals who later rejected him had accepted him for months after the election.

faqs.question: Why did the cardinals turn against Urban VI?
faqs.answer: His abrupt, harsh efforts at reform and his public attacks on the cardinals alienated them. A group of mostly French cardinals then claimed the election had been made under pressure from the Roman mob and was invalid.

faqs.question: What feast did Urban VI add to the Church calendar?
faqs.answer: He decided in 1389 to make the Visitation of the Blessed Virgin Mary a feast for the whole Church. His successor Boniface IX published the decree.

directAnswer: Pope Boniface IX was Pietro Tomacelli, a Neapolitan cardinal elected at a young age on 2 November 1389, who reigned in Rome until 1 October 1404 during the Western Schism. He secured papal control over the city of Rome, celebrated the jubilees of 1390 and 1400, and canonized St. Bridget of Sweden, but his fundraising methods and favoritism toward relatives drew criticism.

sections.h2: A Young Neapolitan Successor to Urban VI
paras: Pietro Tomacelli came from a noble but impoverished family of Naples. Urban VI made him a cardinal in 1381. When Urban died in 1389, the cardinals of the Roman obedience elected Pietro, then in his thirties, a man noted for his gracious manner in contrast with his predecessor.
He reversed Urban's hostility toward the house of Durazzo and recognized the young Ladislaus as king of Naples, having him crowned in 1390. This gave the Roman papacy a vital ally in southern Italy.

sections.h2: Jubilees, the Visitation and St. Bridget
paras: Boniface celebrated the jubilee of 1390 that Urban VI had announced, and pilgrims also came in great numbers in 1400. He published the decree extending the Feast of the Visitation to the whole Church. In 1391 he canonized Bridget of Sweden, the mystic and founder of the Bridgettine Order who had urged the popes to return to Rome.

To raise money in a divided Church, where half of Europe's revenues went to Avignon, he made heavy use of annates, the sale of offices and indulgences granted outside Rome, practices that critics then and later condemned.

sections.h2: Master of Rome in a Divided Church
paras: In 1398 Boniface ended the independence of the Roman commune and placed the city under direct papal government, fortifying Castel Sant'Angelo and the Capitol. He enriched and promoted members of his family.

Efforts to end the schism made no progress. Neither he nor the Avignon claimants, Clement VII and then Benedict XIII, would step aside. Shortly before his death, Boniface received envoys of Benedict XIII but rejected their proposals. He died in Rome on 1 October 1404 and was buried in St. Peter's.

keyFacts: Born Pietro Tomacelli in Naples; cardinal from 1381
Elected in November 1389 by the cardinals of the Roman obedience
Celebrated the jubilees of 1390 and 1400
Canonized St. Bridget of Sweden (1391)
Placed Rome under direct papal rule (1398)
Died in Rome on 1 October 1404

faqs.question: Which saint did Boniface IX canonize?
faqs.answer: He canonized Bridget of Sweden in 1391, eighteen years after her death in Rome.

faqs.question: Why was Boniface IX criticized?
faqs.answer: To fund the Roman papacy during the schism he relied heavily on annates, the sale of offices and indulgences, and he favored his relatives. Many contemporaries saw these as abuses.

directAnswer: Pope Innocent VII was Cosimo de' Migliorati of Sulmona, elected in Rome on 17 October 1404 during the Western Schism; he reigned until his death on 6 November 1406. His two years were troubled by unrest in Rome, and he made little progress toward ending the schism, though he planned the revival of the Roman university with the study of Greek.

sections.h2: Cosimo de' Migliorati, Jurist and Collector
paras: Cosimo de' Migliorati was born at Sulmona in the Abruzzo, then part of the Kingdom of Naples. He studied and taught law, served the curia for years, including in England as a papal collector, and became archbishop of Ravenna and bishop of Bologna. Urban VI made him a cardinal in 1389.
When Boniface IX died, the cardinals of the Roman obedience each swore that, if elected, they would work to end the schism, even by resigning. They chose Cosimo, an elderly man of good reputation.

sections.h2: Rome in Turmoil
paras: Roman factions, encouraged by King Ladislaus of Naples, contested papal authority in the city. In 1405 the pope's nephew Ludovico Migliorati had a group of Roman representatives seized and killed, provoking an uprising that forced Innocent to flee to Viterbo. He returned in 1406 after the Romans submitted to him again.

Innocent planned to restore the University of Rome and to establish teaching in Greek, and the humanist Leonardo Bruni served in his chancery. The schism remained unresolved. He died in Rome on 6 November 1406 and was buried in St. Peter's.

keyFacts: Born Cosimo de' Migliorati at Sulmona, Kingdom of Naples
Canon lawyer; archbishop of Ravenna and bishop of Bologna
Elected 17 October 1404 after swearing to work for the end of the schism
Driven from Rome to Viterbo in 1405 after violence by his nephew
Died in Rome on 6 November 1406

faqs.question: Why did Innocent VII flee Rome?
faqs.answer: In 1405 his nephew Ludovico Migliorati had several Roman representatives killed, sparking a revolt that forced the pope to withdraw to Viterbo. He returned the next year.

faqs.question: Did Innocent VII try to end the Western Schism?
faqs.answer: He had sworn to work for unity, but his short and troubled reign brought no real progress. The schism was ended only at the Council of Constance.

directAnswer: Pope Gregory XII was Angelo Correr of Venice, elected in Rome on 30 November 1406 on a promise to resign if the Avignon claimant would do the same. After years of failed negotiations, he authorized the Council of Constance and resigned on 4 July 1415, opening the way to end the Western Schism. He was the last pope to resign until Benedict XVI in 2013.

sections.h2: An Aged Venetian Elected to End the Schism
paras: Angelo Correr was born in Venice into a noble family. He became bishop of Castello, the see of Venice, and later held the title of Latin Patriarch of Constantinople. Innocent VII made him a cardinal in 1405.

By 1406 pressure to end the schism was intense. The cardinals of the Roman obedience chose Correr, then about eighty, after swearing that the one elected would abdicate if the Avignon claimant, Benedict XIII, also did so, so that a single new pope could be chosen.

sections.h2: Savona, Pisa and Three Rival Claimants
paras: Gregory and Benedict agreed in principle to meet at Savona in 1407, but each found reasons not to complete the journey, and the meeting never took place. Gregory's relatives and the king of Naples were thought to discourage his abdication. When he created new cardinals in 1408 contrary to his promise, most of his cardinals abandoned him.

Cardinals from both obediences then called the Council of Pisa in 1409, which declared both Gregory and Benedict deposed and elected Alexander V. Neither claimant accepted the decision, and Christendom found itself with three rival claimants. Gregory held a council of his own at Cividale and retained the support of a few rulers, including King Ladislaus of Naples for a time and Carlo Malatesta of Rimini.

sections.h2: The Council of Constance and the Resignation of 1415
paras: The Council of Constance was called in 1414 through the efforts of Emperor-elect Sigismund and the Pisan claimant John XXIII. Gregory agreed to resign on condition that he be allowed to convoke the council formally himself. On 4 July 1415, his representative Carlo Malatesta read the bull of convocation and then announced Gregory's resignation.

This procedure preserved the continuity of the Roman line, which the Church regards as the legitimate succession. The council confirmed Gregory's acts, made him cardinal bishop of Porto and legate of the March of Ancona, and later deposed Benedict XIII.

sections.h2: Last Years at Recanati
paras: Gregory spent his final years at Recanati, where he died on 18 October 1417, a few weeks before Martin V was elected and the schism ended. His nephew Gabriele Condulmer, whom he had made a cardinal, would later become Pope Eugene IV.

Elected 30 November 1406 on a pledge to abdicate for the sake of unity
Declared deposed by the Council of Pisa (1409), which he rejected

faqs.question: Why did Gregory XII resign?
faqs.answer: He agreed to step down so the Council of Constance could end the Western Schism, on the condition that he first formally convoke the council. His resignation was announced on 4 July 1415.

faqs.question: Was Gregory XII the last pope to resign before Benedict XVI?
faqs.answer: Yes. No pope resigned between Gregory XII in 1415 and Benedict XVI in 2013.

faqs.question: Why were there three popes during Gregory XII's reign?
faqs.answer: In 1409 the Council of Pisa deposed both Gregory and the Avignon claimant Benedict XIII and elected Alexander V. Neither of the first two accepted this, so three men claimed the papacy until Constance resolved the crisis.

directAnswer: Pope Martin V was Oddone Colonna, a Roman cardinal elected at the Council of Constance on 11 November 1417, whose election effectively ended the Great Western Schism. He reigned until 20 February 1431, re-established the papacy in Rome, rebuilt the city's damaged churches, and dealt cautiously with the conciliar movement and the Hussite crisis in Bohemia.

sections.h2: A Colonna Elected at Constance
paras: Oddone Colonna came from one of Rome's leading families. Innocent VII made him a cardinal in 1405. He supported the Council of Pisa and then followed the Pisan line to the Council of Constance.

After the council had received Gregory XII's resignation and deposed John XXIII and Benedict XIII, a special conclave of twenty-three cardinals and thirty representatives of the council's five nations elected Oddone on 11 November 1417, the feast of St. Martin of Tours, whose name he took. Nearly all of Western Christendom accepted him, and Benedict XIII's following dwindled to a small group in Aragon.

sections.h2: Constance, Frequens and the Councils of Pavia-Siena and Basel
paras: Constance had decreed in Frequens that general councils should meet at regular intervals. Martin honored this by convoking a council at Pavia in 1423, which moved to Siena and achieved little before he dissolved it. He then summoned the next council to Basel for 1431 but died just before it opened.

He also negotiated agreements with the nations represented at Constance on church appointments and finances, restoring much of the papacy's administrative authority while avoiding open conflict over the council's claims to superiority.

sections.h2: Restoring Rome
paras: Martin entered Rome in September 1420 and found it badly decayed after decades of absence and conflict. He restored the papal administration, reasserted control over the Papal States, and began repairs on churches, bridges and walls. At the Lateran he commissioned a new pavement and a fresco cycle begun by Gentile da Fabriano and later completed by Pisanello.

He used his family's power to secure order, granting the Colonna extensive lands and positions. This brought stability during his lifetime but provoked a reaction against the family under his successor.

sections.h2: The Hussite Wars
paras: In Bohemia, the followers of Jan Hus, burned at Constance in 1415, had broken with Rome. In 1420 Martin called for a crusade against them, the first of several campaigns known as the Hussite Wars, which repeatedly failed against the Hussite armies. He appointed Cardinal Giuliano Cesarini to lead the effort and later to preside at Basel.
Martin died in Rome on 20 February 1431. His bronze tomb slab lies before the high altar of the Lateran basilica.

keyFacts: Born Oddone Colonna at Genazzano near Rome; cardinal from 1405
Elected at the Council of Constance on 11 November 1417, ending the schism
Re-entered Rome in 1420 and restored papal government
Convoked the councils of Pavia-Siena (1423) and Basel (1431)

Died 20 February 1431; buried in the Lateran basilica

faqs.question: How did Martin V end the Western Schism?
faqs.answer: He was elected by a special conclave at the Council of Constance after the rival claimants had resigned or been deposed. Almost all of Europe recognized him, leaving only a small remnant loyal to Benedict XIII.

faqs.question: Why did Oddone Colonna choose the name Martin?
faqs.answer: He was elected on 11 November 1417, the feast of St. Martin of Tours.

faqs.question: Did Martin V support the conciliar movement?
faqs.answer: He followed Constance's decree Frequens by calling councils at Pavia-Siena and Basel, but he worked to preserve papal authority and avoided endorsing the claim that councils stood above the pope.

directAnswer: Pope Eugene IV was Gabriele Condulmer of Venice, a nephew of Gregory XII, who reigned from 3 March 1431 to 23 February 1447. His long struggle with the Council of Basel ended with his transfer of the council to Ferrara and Florence, where union with the Greek Orthodox and other Eastern churches was proclaimed in 1439. He also condemned the enslavement of the baptized people of the Canary Islands.

sections.h2: Canon of San Giorgio in Alga
paras: Gabriele Condulmer was born in Venice to a wealthy merchant family. As a young man he gave away much of his inheritance and joined a reform community of canons at San Giorgio in Alga. His uncle Gregory XII made him bishop of Siena and a cardinal in 1408.
Elected in March 1431, he immediately clashed with the Colonna, whose power had grown under Martin V, and with the Council of Basel, which opened that summer.

sections.h2: The Struggle with the Council of Basel
paras: Eugene tried to dissolve the Council of Basel in late 1431, but the council refused and reaffirmed Constance's claim that a general council holds authority even over the pope. Under pressure from Emperor Sigismund, whom he crowned in Rome in May 1433, and from much of Christendom, Eugene withdrew his dissolution later that year.

In 1434 a revolt in Rome forced him to flee the city by boat down the Tiber. He lived for most of the next nine years in Florence, where he consecrated the cathedral of Santa Maria del Fiore with its newly completed dome in 1436. Basel later declared him deposed and in 1439 elected the duke of Savoy as antipope Felix V, but few rulers followed.

sections.h2: Ferrara-Florence and Union with the East
paras: With the Byzantine Empire threatened by the Ottoman Turks, the emperor John VIII Palaiologos sought union with the West. Eugene transferred the council to Ferrara in 1438, where the Greek delegation joined it, and in 1439 moved it to Florence, partly because of plague.

On 6 July 1439 the decree Laetentur caeli proclaimed union between the Latin and Greek churches, affirming the procession of the Holy Spirit and the primacy of the Roman Pontiff. Union decrees with the Armenians and the Copts followed. The union with the Greeks was widely rejected in the East and did not survive the fall of Constantinople, but the council's decrees remained important in Catholic teaching. Eugene also supported the crusade that ended in defeat at Varna in 1444.

sections.h2: Sicut Dudum and the Canary Islands
paras: In the 1430s reports reached Eugene that Christian raiders were enslaving inhabitants of the Canary Islands, including those already baptized. In the bull Sicut dudum of January 1435, following earlier measures in 1434, he ordered that such captives be set free within a set time under penalty of excommunication.
Eugene returned to Rome in 1443 and died there on 23 February 1447. He had made peace with the German princes shortly before his death, a step toward the end of the Basel schism under his successor.

keyFacts: Born Gabriele Condulmer in Venice; nephew of Gregory XII
Canon regular of San Giorgio in Alga; cardinal from 1408
Crowned Emperor Sigismund in Rome (1433)
Transferred the council from Basel to Ferrara (1438) and Florence (1439)
Proclaimed union with the Greeks in Laetentur caeli (1439)
Condemned enslavement of baptized Canary Islanders in Sicut dudum (1435)

faqs.question: What was the Council of Florence?
faqs.answer: It was the general council Eugene IV moved from Basel to Ferrara in 1438 and then to Florence in 1439. There the Latin Church and the Byzantine delegation proclaimed reunion, though the union was later rejected in the East.

faqs.question: Why did Eugene IV live in Florence?
faqs.answer: A revolt in Rome in 1434 forced him to flee. He spent most of the following years in Florence, returning to Rome only in 1443.

faqs.question: What did Eugene IV say about slavery in the Canary Islands?
faqs.answer: In Sicut dudum (1435) he ordered that baptized Canary Islanders who had been enslaved be freed within a fixed period, on pain of excommunication for those who held them.

directAnswer: Pope Nicholas V was Tommaso Parentucelli of Sarzana, a humanist scholar who reigned from 6 March 1447 to 24 March 1455. He ended the Basel schism, held the jubilee of 1450, crowned Frederick III as emperor in Rome in 1452, and founded the collection that became the Vatican Library. His reign also saw the fall of Constantinople and bulls granting Portugal rights of conquest in Africa.

sections.h2: A Humanist Scholar Becomes Pope
paras: Tommaso Parentucelli was born at Sarzana in Liguria, the son of a physician. He studied at Bologna and spent many years in the household of Cardinal Niccolò Albergati, traveling with him and building a deep knowledge of books. At Cosimo de' Medici's request he drew up a plan for organizing the library of San Marco in Florence.

Eugene IV made him bishop of Bologna in 1444 and a cardinal in 1446 after a successful mission to the German princes. A year later he was elected pope and took the name Nicholas in honor of Albergati, whose baptismal name was Niccolò.

sections.h2: Ending the Basel Schism and Crowning Frederick III
paras: Nicholas reached the Concordat of Vienna with Frederick III in 1448, settling church appointments in the Empire. In 1449 the antipope Felix V resigned and the remnant of the Council of Basel dissolved itself, bringing the conciliar schism to a close.

In 1450 Nicholas celebrated a jubilee that drew great numbers of pilgrims to Rome, and that year he canonized St. Bernardino of Siena. On 19 March 1452 he crowned Frederick III emperor in St. Peter's, the last imperial coronation to take place in Rome.

sections.h2: The Vatican Library and the Renewal of Rome
paras: Nicholas gathered manuscripts from across Europe and the East, employed scholars to translate Greek works into Latin, and left a collection of over a thousand volumes. This became the foundation of the Vatican Library, formally organized under Sixtus IV.

He also planned a broad renewal of Rome: repairing walls, aqueducts and churches, and beginning work on a new choir for St. Peter's. Fra Angelico painted the scenes of Sts. Stephen and Lawrence in his private chapel, now called the Niccoline Chapel.

sections.h2: Constantinople, the Crusade and the Portuguese Bulls
paras: Constantinople fell to Sultan Mehmed II on 29 May 1453. Nicholas called for a crusade to recover it, but the powers of Europe did not respond in force. The same year he survived a conspiracy led by the Roman Stefano Porcari, who was executed.

In 1452 he issued Dum diversas, authorizing King Afonso V of Portugal to attack and subdue Saracens and pagans and to reduce them to perpetual servitude, and in 1455 Romanus Pontifex confirmed Portuguese rights in Africa. These bulls are today seen as part of the history of European colonization and the slave trade, and the Holy See addressed this history in a 2023 statement on the so-called doctrine of discovery. Nicholas died in Rome on 24 March 1455.

keyFacts: Born Tommaso Parentucelli at Sarzana; humanist and book collector
Ended the Basel schism with Felix V's resignation (1449)
Held the jubilee of 1450 and canonized St. Bernardino of Siena
Crowned Frederick III in Rome (1452), the last imperial coronation there
Founded the collection that became the Vatican Library
Issued Dum diversas (1452); pope at the fall of Constantinople (1453)

faqs.question: Did Nicholas V found the Vatican Library?
faqs.answer: He assembled the large collection of manuscripts that formed its foundation and intended it as a library open to scholars. The library was formally organized under Sixtus IV in 1475.

faqs.question: What was Dum diversas?
faqs.answer: A 1452 bull of Nicholas V authorizing the king of Portugal to conquer Saracens and pagans and reduce them to servitude. It is now studied as part of the history of colonization and slavery, and the Holy See addressed it in a 2023 statement.

faqs.question: Why is Nicholas V's coronation of Frederick III significant?
faqs.answer: Frederick III's coronation in St. Peter's in 1452 was the last time a Holy Roman Emperor was crowned in Rome.

directAnswer: Pope Callixtus III was Alfonso de Borja of Xàtiva, the first pope from the Kingdom of Valencia and the first of the Borgia family, who reigned from 8 April 1455 to 6 August 1458. He devoted his pontificate to a crusade against the Ottomans, ordered the retrial that vindicated Joan of Arc, and extended the Feast of the Transfiguration to the whole Church.

sections.h2: Alfonso de Borja, Jurist of Aragon
paras: Alfonso de Borja was born at Xàtiva near Valencia. He studied and taught law at Lleida and entered the service of King Alfonso V of Aragon. He helped bring about the submission of Clement VIII, successor to Benedict XIII's line, in 1429, ending the last remnant of the Western Schism, and was rewarded with the bishopric of Valencia.
Eugene IV made him a cardinal in 1444. When Nicholas V died, the cardinals, divided between the Colonna and Orsini factions, elected Alfonso, then about seventy-six, as a compromise.

sections.h2: The Crusade and the Relief of Belgrade
paras: Two years after the fall of Constantinople, Callixtus made the war against the Ottomans his central concern. He sent preachers across Europe, levied taxes for the crusade and built a papal fleet. In 1456 he ordered church bells to be rung at midday to call the faithful to pray for the defenders of Christendom, a practice linked to the later noonday Angelus bell.

In July 1456 the Hungarian commander John Hunyadi, with crusaders inspired by the Franciscan St. John of Capistrano, broke the Ottoman siege of Belgrade. When news of the victory reached Rome on 6 August, Callixtus extended the Feast of the Transfiguration, kept on that date, to the universal Church, a decree issued in 1457.

sections.h2: The Rehabilitation of Joan of Arc
paras: Joan of Arc had been condemned and burned at Rouen in 1431. At the request of her mother and family, and with the support of the French crown, Callixtus authorized a new inquiry in 1455. On 7 July 1456 the papal commissioners declared the original trial null and void, clearing her name. Joan was canonized much later, in 1920.
In 1455 he also canonized the Dominican preacher St. Vincent Ferrer, a fellow Valencian.

sections.h2: Nepotism and the Borgia Rise
paras: Callixtus brought many Catalans and Valencians to Rome and promoted his relatives. In 1456 he made two nephews cardinals, among them Rodrigo de Borja, who would later become Pope Alexander VI, and he gave another nephew high military command in the Papal States. These appointments caused resentment among the Romans.
He died in Rome on 6 August 1458, the feast he had extended to the whole Church.

keyFacts: Born Alfonso de Borja at Xàtiva; first Valencian pope and first Borgia pope
Former bishop of Valencia and adviser to Alfonso V of Aragon
Ordered midday bells and prayers for the crusade; Belgrade relieved in 1456
Extended the Feast of the Transfiguration (6 August) to the universal Church
Authorized the retrial that annulled Joan of Arc's condemnation (1456)
Made his nephew Rodrigo, the future Alexander VI, a cardinal; died 6 August 1458

faqs.question: How did Callixtus III help Joan of Arc?
faqs.answer: He authorized a new inquiry into her case in 1455. In July 1456 papal commissioners declared her 1431 condemnation null and void.

faqs.question: Why is the Transfiguration celebrated on 6 August?
faqs.answer: The feast was already kept on that date in many places. Callixtus III made it universal after news of the victory at Belgrade reached Rome on 6 August 1456.

faqs.question: Was Callixtus III related to Pope Alexander VI?
faqs.answer: Yes. Rodrigo de Borja, who became Alexander VI in 1492, was his nephew, and Callixtus made him a cardinal in 1456.

directAnswer: Pope Pius II was Enea Silvio Piccolomini of Corsignano near Siena, a celebrated humanist writer and former supporter of the Council of Basel, who reigned from 19 August 1458 to 14 August 1464. He condemned appeals from the pope to a future council, canonized St. Catherine of Siena, rebuilt his birthplace as the town of Pienza, and wrote the Commentaries, the only autobiography written by a reigning pope.

sections.h2: Enea Silvio, Humanist and Diplomat
paras: Enea Silvio Piccolomini was born in 1405 at Corsignano, in the territory of Siena, to an impoverished noble family. He studied at Siena and Florence and became known for elegant Latin prose and poetry. He went to the Council of Basel as a secretary, served the antipope Felix V, and later joined the chancery of Emperor Frederick III, who crowned him poet laureate in 1442.

In his early years he wrote secular works, including a popular love story in Latin and a comedy, and he fathered children. In the mid-1440s he reconciled with Eugene IV, was ordained a priest in 1446, and became bishop of Trieste and then of Siena. Callixtus III made him a cardinal in 1456.

sections.h2: Execrabilis and the Retraction of His Conciliarist Past
paras: As pope, Pius defended the authority he had once questioned. In the bull Execrabilis of 1460 he condemned appeals from the pope to a future general council, declaring them void. In 1463, in a bull addressed to the University of Cologne, he retracted his own earlier writings in favor of the council, asking readers to reject the young Aeneas and accept Pius.
He also canonized St. Catherine of Siena in 1461, an act that carried special meaning for a son of Siena.

sections.h2: The Congress of Mantua and the Last Crusade
paras: Pius made a crusade against the Ottoman Turks the chief aim of his reign. In 1459 he summoned Christian rulers to a congress at Mantua, but attendance was poor and pledges were few. A letter addressed to Sultan Mehmed II, inviting him to accept baptism, survives among his writings, though it is uncertain whether it was ever sent.

In 1464 Pius took the cross himself and traveled to Ancona to lead the crusade in person. The promised fleets were slow to arrive, and he died at Ancona on 14 August 1464 before the expedition could depart.

sections.h2: Pienza and the Commentaries
paras: Pius had his birthplace rebuilt by the architect Bernardo Rossellino as a planned Renaissance town, with a cathedral, papal palace and square designed as a unified whole. In 1462 he renamed it Pienza after himself and made it a bishopric. Its center is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

His Commentaries, written in the third person, describe his life, travels, the politics of his time and the landscapes of Italy with unusual vividness. They remain a major source for fifteenth-century history and the only memoir composed by a pope during his reign. His earlier works include descriptions of Germany, Bohemia and Europe.

keyFacts: Born Enea Silvio Piccolomini at Corsignano near Siena in 1405
Humanist author, crowned poet laureate by Frederick III (1442)
Condemned appeals to a future council in Execrabilis (1460)
Canonized St. Catherine of Siena (1461)
Rebuilt Corsignano as Pienza (1462) and wrote the Commentaries
Died at Ancona on 14 August 1464 while preparing a crusade

faqs.question: What are the Commentaries of Pius II?
faqs.answer: They are his memoirs, written in the third person during his pontificate. They describe his life and times in detail and are the only autobiography written by a reigning pope.

faqs.question: Why did Pius II retract his earlier writings?
faqs.answer: As a young man at the Council of Basel he had argued that a general council was superior to the pope. As pope he publicly withdrew those views in 1463, asking readers to reject Aeneas and accept Pius.

faqs.question: What is Pienza?
faqs.answer: It is his birthplace, Corsignano, which he had rebuilt as an ideal Renaissance town by Bernardo Rossellino and renamed Pienza in 1462.
